Problem 256. The best route from Iris to Zephyr
A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.
Iris–Quartz–Zephyr has segment costs [4, 5] (total 9); Iris–Riverbend–Yarrow–Zephyr has segment costs [3, 2, 4] (total 9); Iris–Birch–Zephyr has segment costs [7, 2] (total 9).
A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.
Which route should a traveler use from Iris to Zephyr, and why?
1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. All listed routes are open. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 9, on Iris–Quartz–Zephyr.
A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.
Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

Problem 261. Following water from North Fork
River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.
North Fork flows into Willow Stream; Blue Creek flows into Willow Stream; Willow Stream flows into Clearwater.
If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.
Is North Fork upstream of Clearwater? Can water from North Fork reach Clearwater through the stated network?

1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: North Fork→Willow Stream, Blue Creek→Willow Stream, Willow Stream→Clearwater. 2. Follow arrows starting from North Fork. 3. An arrow path reaches Clearwater, so North Fork is upstream of Clearwater.
Yes; water from North Fork can reach Clearwater.
A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.
Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.
